1287| **Theorem 10.** Let the rows of $X^{\mathrm r}$ be i.i.d. $N_p(m_n,\Sigma_n)$ with $\Sigma_n$ a correlation matrix, and
1288| $y^{\mathrm r}=\alpha\mathbf 1+X\theta^*+\varepsilon$ with a deterministic $\theta^*$. Assume
1289| - **(A1) Model and method.** (S1), (S2), (S3), (S5); $p>s_0$.
1290| - **(A2) Sparsity and fixed signals.** $s_0\ge1$ fixed; $\theta_{\mathrm{lo}}\le|\theta^*_j|\le\theta_{\mathrm{hi}}$ on $S_0$.
1291| - **(A3) Population sparse eigenvalue floor.** $\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{n,S})\ge c>0$ for every $|S|\le5(A+1)(s_0+1)\log n$.
1292| - **(A4) Visibility** and **(A5) no leakage**: (A4) and (A5) of Theorem 5.
1293| 
1294| *Which designs.* (A5) holds only for designs with no leakage outside the true model, such as independent predictors.
1295| AR and block designs, where a null is correlated with a truth at a fixed level, are **not** covered. For those designs
1296| Theorem 6 (row 3.1, the reported model is $S_0$) still applies under its own conditions, and the pooled evidence is
1297| unbiased for every design (row 3.5, remark below); consistency of the printed PIPs, MPM and $\hat Z$ is not claimed
1298| there.
1299| 
1300| This theorem concerns the sampler branch of the method (the model space is too large to enumerate; the exact branch is
1301| the scope note below). Let $\mathcal A$ be the event that the method takes the sampler branch and its calibration
1302| succeeds (fallback ladder included); every completed sampler run lies in $\mathcal A$. On $\mathcal A$ let $\hat Z$,
1303| $\widehat{\mathrm{PIP}}$, $\widehat{\mathrm{MPM}}$ denote the evidence estimate, pooled PIPs and their MPM computed from the
1304| four islands' uninterrupted records (equal-weight pooling, `NOTATION.md` §5); on completed runs they are exactly the
1305| printed fields, and $\hat S$ is the reported model. Let $\rho_n:=n^{-1/2}e^{C\sqrt{\log n}}$ for a suitable constant $C$
1306| (so $\rho_n\le n^{-c}$ eventually, for every $c<\tfrac12$). Then, under the joint law of design, noise and the method's
1307| random numbers,

1311| $$
1312| P\big(\mathcal A\cap\{\widehat{\mathrm{MPM}}\neq S_0\}\big)\to0,\qquad P\big(\text{the run completes and }\hat S\neq S_0\big)\to0 ,
1313| $$

  10| 
  11| We observe a response vector $y^{\mathrm r}\in\mathbb R^n$ and an $n\times p_{\mathrm{raw}}$ matrix of predictors
  12| $X^{\mathrm r}$. Predictor columns that are constant are removed by the method before anything else is computed; $p$
  13| denotes the number of **retained** (non-constant) columns, indexed by $[p]=\{1,\dots,p\}$.
  14| 
  15| **Model.** The data follow a Gaussian linear model with an intercept,
  16| $$
  17| y^{\mathrm r}=\alpha^*\mathbf 1_n+X^{\mathrm r}\beta^*+\varepsilon,\qquad \varepsilon\sim N_n(0,\sigma_*^2 I_n),
  18| $$
  19| with $\sigma_*^2>0$ and $\varepsilon$ independent of $X^{\mathrm r}$. Two kinds of design are considered.
  20| 
  21| * **Fixed design.** $X^{\mathrm r}$ is deterministic; probability refers to $\varepsilon$ only.
  22| * **Random Gaussian design.** The rows of $X^{\mathrm r}$ are i.i.d. $N_p(m_n,\Sigma_n)$. Since the method standardises
  23|   every column (§2), we may and do take $\Sigma_n$ to be a **correlation matrix** (unit diagonal). Probability then
  24|   refers to the joint law of $(X^{\mathrm r},\varepsilon)$. A generic population row is written
  25|   $W=(W_1,\dots,W_p)\sim N_p(0,\Sigma_n)$ (the mean plays no role).
  26| 
  27| **Truth.** $S_0:=\operatorname{supp}\beta^*=\{j:\beta^*_j\neq 0\}$ is the true model, $s_0:=|S_0|$ its size.

  31| Let $C:=I_n-\tfrac1n\mathbf 1\mathbf 1^\top$ be the centring matrix and $D$ the diagonal matrix of the sample standard
